entries.title: When your child turns down help
entries.summary: During an activity, an offer of help can be refused. Davies makes room for the frustration and anger that may follow, and for another chance to try later.
entries.cue: Your child is struggling with an activity but pushes away your hand or says they do not want help.
detail: Davies suggests offering a small demonstration or a short cue when a child is about to give up. If they welcome it, the adult helps with that part and then sees how the child continues.

Sometimes the child refuses every offer and becomes angry. In the book’s account, that feeling is allowed too; the activity can wait for another attempt. The child need not accept a demonstration or finish the task now.

This discussion concerns an activity the child is exploring. Supervision still applies to small parts and sharp objects, and the adult’s responsibility for necessary care or immediate protection remains.

A known limit need not receive lengthy renegotiation each time; laughter does not remove the limit.

qualifications: Examples include heat, outlets, road access, going too far unattended and climbing by windows.
If the child returns repeatedly, consider changing access or removing the hazard.
The source’s box-over-outlet, couch-before-wires and locked-room cabinet examples lack implementation specifications; they are not blanket home-safety approvals.

qualifications: Observe what is repeated; allow another turn and provide related challenge.
Offer fewer activities and rotate ones too easy/hard or persistently unused/thrown.
Respond when the child looks for adult contact; language-rich conversation can happen at other daily moments.
Give small help near giving up, then step back; a key/box example illustrates partial help.
A mat or table can support focus before work begins, but do not interrupt a child already concentrating at the shelf to move them.

qualifications: Examples: slowly demonstrate turning a puzzle piece or suggest turning it.
The child may refuse help and feel angry; trying later is allowed.
Rosary-bead anecdote explains adult restraint, not a child activity.
Pausing does not apply to immediate danger194.

The refusal concerns an explored activity, not all necessary care or protection. No need to complete the activity or accept a lesson in the moment. Frustration and anger are not failure; help stays available.
provenance.illustrationImplications: No image required. Any future image must not imply the adult forces a hand into a task or withdraws needed care.
provenance.sensitivity: Ordinary activity support with explicit care/protection boundary; no therapeutic claims.
